- Overestimate early in the forecast horizon when sentiment is negative (especially > -0.40), as models tend to underreact to bearish signals.
- Underestimate when sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., > 0.30) — models often overreact to bullish sentiment, leading to lagged or delayed price spikes.
- Avoid sharp downward forecasts when recent sentiment is mildly negative (e.g., -0.10 to -0.30) — true outcomes often show mean reversion or slight rebound.
- Overshoot after spikes: if model forecasts a sharp peak followed by a drop, actual price often continues upward or stabilizes — don’t assume momentum reverses.
- Mean reversion bias: if model consistently forecasts prices below 65–68 range after 3–5 days of high sentiment, actual price often rebounds — adjust downward bias by 2–3% for 3-day horizon.
- Horizon-specific: 30-day forecasts are prone to underestimating late-period spikes (especially after 20–25 days) — add 1–2% buffer for sentiment-driven late rallies.
- Lagged sentiment effect: if sentiment is negative for 3+ consecutive days, model should not forecast a 30-day peak — instead, expect a 10–15 day lagged correction.
